chunks: From wafer to packaged chip. The question: What is the process from wafer to chip?
After a wafer is fully processed, all its chips are still joined together. To make usable parts, each die is first tested on the wafer. The wafer is then thinned and cut apart.
The good dies are placed in packages and connected, and the packaged parts are tested again and sorted by performance.
The order exists so that you never spend packaging money on a die that does not work.
Think of a fruit packing house. Workers inspect fruit before it goes into boxes, because a box and its labor are wasted on spoiled fruit.
A final check at the end catches anything damaged during packing. Chips get the same two checks: one on the bare die and one on the packaged part.
Everything up to dicing is done on the whole wafer in parallel; after dicing, work proceeds one die or one strip of packages at a time, so cost scales with unit count.
Wafer probe: testing each die on the wafer with tiny needles that touch its pads. Dicing: cutting the wafer apart into individual dies with a saw or laser.
Package: the case around the die, with connections to the board. Wire bond or flip chip: two ways to connect the die to the package. and "What are flip chips?"
Binning: sorting finished parts into grades, such as fast and slow.
Say a die costs 2. 00 currency units to make and 1. 00 to package, and 90% of dies work. Without probing, you package everything. The cost per good part is (2. 00 + 1. 00) ÷ 0.
9 about 3. 33. With probing, you package only good dies. The cost per good part is 2. 00 ÷ 0. 9 + 1. 00 about 3. 22.
The saving is about 3% here, and it grows when packaging is expensive. That is why multi-die packages insist on testing each die first. That is the whole idea.
"After processing, you probe-test every die on the wafer and map the good ones.
Then the wafer is thinned by back-grinding, mounted on tape and diced into individual dies with a saw or laser.
Good dies are attached to a lead frame or substrate, connected by wire bonds or flip-chip bumps, encapsulated in mould compound, and finished with leads or solder balls.
Final test and binning sort the parts by performance before they ship."
